sourcePolicy: Each item is an attributable and located authorial interpretation. Bible anchors remain subject to exact Vulgate/Crampon/1962 text collation; source passages do not in themselves prove ritual origins.

records.attributableClaim: Psalm 42 is selected around the altar-approach verse; Guéranger also reads it christologically. Verify Psalm 42/43 edition numbering.
Guéranger expressly compares breast-striking during the Confiteor with the publican's penitence; this comparison is not a claim that the Confiteor was authored in Luke.
The verse from Psalm 84/85 asks God to show mercy and grant salvation; Guéranger offers a Christological reading.
The priest's ascent is described with sanctuary language; Guéranger likens the approach to the Holy of Holies. This is theological analogy, not evidence of an identical Temple ritual.
Guéranger explicitly invokes the angel with golden censer and prayers of the saints in the Apocalypse when interpreting incense.
Guéranger explains the original chant role and its later recital by priests with the development of Low Mass; historical dates and exact evolution still need Jungmann/Le Brun checks.
Guéranger interprets groups of three invocations in a Trinitarian way and relates the nine utterances to the nine choirs; no claim of direct biblical quotation.

records.liturgicalAnchor: Gloria in excelsis Deo, et in terra pax
records.attributableClaim: The angelic announcement forms the opening; the later hymn includes substantially more text than the Gospel verse.
Guéranger reads the Christological title in the Gloria through John the Baptist's testimony.

records.biblicalReferences: 1 Timothy 4:13 (illustrative, not a reading fixed for every Mass)
records.attributableClaim: Guéranger contrasts an older multiple-lesson order with the ordinary later one-lesson order; no fixed scriptural passage exists for the epistle slot.
The Gradual is a responsorial chant associated with the ambo steps; Guéranger separates historical naming from the biblical Psalms of ascent.
Guéranger explains the distinct Gospel proclamation and the ministerial roles; neither epistle nor Gospel is one unchanging biblical episode.

Guéranger gives an account of the Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed's adoption at Rome; compare dates and contents with documentary research. Creed is a conciliar formulation, not a verbatim biblical passage.
Guéranger explicitly connects the unblemished-host wording with Old Testament unblemished offerings and with Christ; textual allusions require individual verse collation.
Guéranger connects the creation of humanity and participation in divine nature to the prayer over the water and wine.

records.liturgicalAnchor: Water mixed with wine: the people and Christ
records.attributableClaim: Cyprian insists on mixed wine and water, reading wine in relation to Christ's blood and water to the people united with Him. This is not identical to Guéranger's water/humanity, wine/divinity explanation.

sources.author: St Cyprian, Letter to Caecilius (New Advent numbering Ep.62)

records.attributableClaim: The offering of the chalice echoes the psalm's cup of salvation; classify as candidate allusion pending exact 1962 Latin / Vulgate collation.
Traditional scriptural wording of humble/contrite spirit and acceptable sacrifice. Exact verse numbering across Catholic editions remains on hold.

records.liturgicalAnchor: Suscipe sancta Trinitas ob memoriam Passionis Resurrectionis et Ascensionis
records.attributableClaim: Guéranger treats Passion, Resurrection and Ascension as the three explicitly named mysteries of salvation in the Offertory prayer, not an assertion that the formula is a Gospel quotation.

records.liturgicalAnchor: Dirigatur Domine oratio mea sicut incensum
records.attributableClaim: The Offertory incense prayer quotes Psalm 140/141. Check Solemn / sung distinctions and place this passage in the actual incensation phase.
Guéranger explicitly identifies Psalm 25 and distinguishes practical handwashing after incense from purification symbolism.

records.liturgicalAnchor: Sursum corda; Gratias agamus Domino Deo nostro
records.attributableClaim: Guéranger describes thanksgiving and union with the angels in the Preface. Do not manufacture a literal Bible citation for the introductory dialogue.

sources.author: St Thomas Aquinas, ST III q.83
sources.locator: a.4 body, Preface and people's prayer

records.liturgicalAnchor: Sanctus Sanctus Sanctus Dominus Deus Sabaoth
records.attributableClaim: The heavenly acclamation in Isaiah is recited in the Sanctus; Revelation 4:8 is a parallel vision, not the source of every word in the Roman formula.

sources.author: St Thomas Aquinas, ST III q.83

records.attributableClaim: Guéranger explicitly juxtaposes Isaiah and St John's Apocalypse; create a second, parallel episode link rather than fusing their visions.

records.liturgicalAnchor: Benedictus qui venit in nomine Domini
records.attributableClaim: This acclamation is presented in Guéranger as the crowd's blessing at the entry into Jerusalem; Psalm 117 supplies prior biblical wording.

sources.author: St Thomas Aquinas, ST III q.83

records.liturgicalAnchor: Te igitur ... pro Ecclesia tua sancta catholica
records.attributableClaim: Guéranger explains prayer for unity of the Church and links it to the scriptural vision of unity; the Latin Canon prayer is not a verbatim quotation from John 17.
Prayer for the living in the Canon corresponds to intercession for others; Aquinas explains the prayer for the Church and particular persons.

sources.author: St Thomas Aquinas, ST III q.83

records.liturgicalAnchor: Hanc igitur oblationem, hands held over offerings
records.attributableClaim: Guéranger relates the extension of hands to Old Law hand-imposition over victims. This is an explicit traditional interpretation, not sufficient historical evidence that one gesture was directly inherited from the other.
Aquinas interprets 'rational' as a moral/spiritual transformation of the faithful; a citation to Romans 12 is a theme requiring further source collation, not a direct textual derivation.

sources.author: St Thomas Aquinas, ST III q.83

records.liturgicalAnchor: Qui pridie ... Hoc est enim Corpus meum
records.attributableClaim: The Roman institution narrative is rooted in scriptural institution accounts, but the 1962 Latin formula must be collated against each account word by word; not a verbatim duplicate of any one Gospel.

sources.author: St Thomas Aquinas, ST III q.83

records.liturgicalAnchor: Hic est enim calix sanguinis mei ... pro multis
records.attributableClaim: The Roman cup formula synthesises scriptural Last Supper expressions in received liturgical form; a four-text comparison is required, particularly for 'mysterium fidei'.

records.liturgicalAnchor: Unde et memores ... Passionis Resurrectionis Ascensionis
records.attributableClaim: The liturgy expressly commemorates the Passion, Resurrection and Ascension; do not reduce anamnesis to replaying only the Last Supper.

sources.author: St Thomas Aquinas, ST III q.83

records.attributableClaim: Abel's accepted gift is named by the Roman Canon; Guéranger distinguishes the ancient offering from Christ's sacrifice.

sources.author: St Thomas Aquinas, ST III q.83

records.attributableClaim: Abraham's obedient offering and the substitute ram are narrated in Genesis; Guéranger contrasts his consent with Christ's perfect self-offering.

records.liturgicalAnchor: quod tibi obtulit summus sacerdos tuus Melchisedech
records.attributableClaim: Melchizedek is expressly named. Cyprian §4 and Ambrose §§45–46 interpret the priest and bread/wine christologically; the Genesis account itself does not explain all of the later typology.

sources.author: St Cyprian, Letter to Caecilius (New Advent numbering Ep.62)

records.attributableClaim: Guéranger relates this prayer to the Lamb and heavenly altar in Revelation. Aquinas explicitly disallows a literal physical transport of the Eucharistic species; his explanation is spiritual/ecclesial.

sources.author: St Thomas Aquinas, ST III q.83

records.liturgicalAnchor: Memento etiam Domine ... qui nos praecesserunt
records.attributableClaim: The Mass prays for the departed; the deuterocanonical text provides a Catholic scriptural rationale for prayer for the dead, not the source of these exact words.

sources.author: St Thomas Aquinas, ST III q.83

records.attributableClaim: Guéranger proposes a historical account involving blessing produce during the Canon; documentation must be checked critically with primary ritual witnesses and Jungmann before giving as fact.
Guéranger cites Christ's instruction and discusses the petitions. The introductions and liturgical arrangement are distinct from the Gospel texts.

sources.author: St Thomas Aquinas, ST III q.83

records.liturgicalAnchor: Haec commixtio et consecratio Corporis et Sanguinis
records.attributableClaim: Guéranger reads the mixture as a sign of reunion of the risen Christ's Body and Blood; this is one traditional devotional exposition, not the demonstrated historical purpose of the ritual.

records.liturgicalAnchor: Agnus Dei qui tollis peccata mundi
records.attributableClaim: Guéranger identifies the Baptist's words and contrasts the Mass's response and prayers for peace and repose.

records.liturgicalAnchor: Pacem relinquo vobis pacem meam do vobis
records.attributableClaim: The priest's Communion preparation prayer expressly cites Christ's words on peace, interpreted by Guéranger through Eucharistic communion.

records.liturgicalAnchor: Domine non sum dignus ut intres sub tectum meum
records.attributableClaim: The centurion's request becomes an adapted first-person prayer for healing of the soul before Communion.

records.liturgicalAnchor: In principio erat Verbum ... Et Verbum caro factum est
records.attributableClaim: Guéranger identifies the Johannine Prologue and describes the later devotion and medieval origin of the Last Gospel. The Gospel source is direct, but its placement at the end of Mass is historical development.

records.liturgicalAnchor: Kneeling at Et Verbum caro factum est
records.attributableClaim: Guéranger explicitly connects the genuflection to the Incarnation and the self-emptying of the Word; not proof that the gesture itself was appointed in the apostolic era.

Ambrose §47–49 deliberately contrasts perishable manna with the Eucharist; this is a patristic type available to a broader Eucharistic formation module, not a direct quotation in a fixed part of Mass.

Cyprian §4 explicitly argues for Melchizedek as prefiguration of Christ's sacrifice and Ambrose §45–46 treats Christ as priestly fulfilment. Keep distinct from M035's claim about the Canon's own words.

sources.author: St Cyprian, Letter to Caecilius (New Advent numbering Ep.62)

records.attributableClaim: Ambrose §43 applies the Psalm 'I will go to the altar of God' to newly initiated Christians approaching the Eucharistic altar; do not claim this is an historical origin of the 1962 foot-of-altar prayers.

records.liturgicalAnchor: Haec dona haec munera haec sancta sacrificia illibata
records.attributableClaim: Durandus offers multiple non-exclusive interpretations of three crosses: Trinity, stages before Moses, Passion-related meanings, and more. The specific pre-Mosaic genealogy of Adam→Noah→Abraham→Moses is his medieval symbolic scheme, not an actual linear history of the Roman Canon.

sources.author: Guillaume Durand (Durandus), Rationale IV, French trans. Charles Barthélemy 1854

records.attributableClaim: Durandus explicitly says that recognition of the Lord in the breaking of the bread at Emmaus illuminates the fraction; unlike a direct Mass quotation, this is a medieval authorial comparison.

sources.author: Guillaume Durand (Durandus), Rationale IV, French trans. Charles Barthélemy 1854
sources.locator: Book IV chapter 51, section on breaking the bread

records.attributableClaim: Durandus offers a resurrection/return-of-the-soul interpretation for the commixture, while also recounting distinct medieval sequences for doing it. That variation is itself evidence against a timeless single symbol-to-rubric explanation.

sources.author: Guillaume Durand (Durandus), Rationale IV, French trans. Charles Barthélemy 1854
Dom Prosper Guéranger, Explication (1885)
sources.locator: Commixture, second part of the Mass

records.liturgicalAnchor: mysterium fidei in the consecration formula
records.attributableClaim: Durandus attributes to Innocent III the observation that the Gospel writers did not use the precise phrase mysterium fidei. Do not invent a Gospel verse containing the phrase; mark the Roman formula and the biblical institution accounts as distinct.

sources.author: Guillaume Durand (Durandus), Rationale IV, French trans. Charles Barthélemy 1854

records.liturgicalAnchor: Canon divisions: Te igitur; Memento; Communicantes ...
records.attributableClaim: Durandus reports rival divisions of the Canon into 11, 12, 6 and 5 textual groups. These are medieval analytical schemes, not the modern Mass-reading card count; never impose one medieval structure over the app's liturgical source-first arrangement.

sources.author: Guillaume Durand (Durandus), Rationale IV, French trans. Charles Barthélemy 1854

records.liturgicalAnchor: Te igitur and the Holy of Holies
records.attributableClaim: Durandus connects the prayer of the priest, the Temple high priest and Christ entering the heavenly sanctuary. The prayer's genuine liturgical language and later interpretative image must remain visibly separate.

sources.author: Guillaume Durand (Durandus), Rationale IV, French trans. Charles Barthélemy 1854

criticalMethodWitness.author: Pierre Le Brun, Preface (1843 ed.)
criticalMethodWitness.locator: Discussion of gesture meaning, against theatrically literal gesturing and purely practical rationalism

holds.note: Guéranger claims the Roman Canon has always remained the same everywhere; do not state this as history: compare early Sacramentaries, 1962 wording and Jungmann/Fortescue.
Attributions to Popes Alexander I/Leo/Gregory for adding exact Canon phrases need manuscript and historical verification.
holds.loc: Qui pridie 515; Supra quae 577; Hanc igitur 501

holds.note: Cyprian reads water as people and wine as Christ's blood, while Guéranger emphasizes humanity/divinity and incorporation; retain both named interpretations separately.
Guéranger explicitly rejects interpreting every gesture as an incident of the Passion.
Guéranger notes and questions attribution of the Gloria to St Hilary; do not assign as fact.
Later addition: although exact John 1 wording is scriptural, the Last Gospel's liturgical placement is medieval, with numerous historical particularities.
Aquinas rejects physical transportation of consecrated species in Supplices; prevent literal cinematics of angel carrying Christ's body to heaven.
holds.loc: III q.83 a.4 Reply to Obj.9

holds.note: Crampon/Douay/Vulgate numbering differences in Daniel 3 Greek addition and Psalms: edition crosswalk required.
Source texts date to earlier Roman liturgical usages, sometimes inaccurate about 1962 Holy Week, Joseph in Canon, rubrics. Compare canonical project 1962 Mass text for every record before rendering.
Guéranger's 'reunion of Body and Blood' for commixture is attributed interpretation and is not an archaeological/historical explanation.
Durandus gives several competing symbolic explanations for the same three signs of the Cross, proof that the medieval text is not a unique historical explanation.
Durandus does relate the Eucharistic fraction to Emmaus, but this is medieval exegesis; do not assert the Rite of Fraction was founded to depict Emmaus.
holds.loc: Book IV ch.51, paragraph on recognition at Emmaus

holds.note: Historical liturgical ‘mysterium fidei’ is not a literal phrase of the four biblical institution passages; keep Roman Canon words and exact Gospel wording apart.
